messages.content:
# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

messages.content:
# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

Where a state requires a background check on every sale, where it gives families a court to turn to when someone is in crisis, and where it restricts the weapons built to kill many people quickly, fewer children die. The rest of this brief sets out the two federal policies that would move those protections from a patchwork of state laws to the whole country.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check on every firearm sold by a licensed dealer. The requirement stops at the dealer's counter. In most states a private seller may hand a gun to a stranger, at a kitchen table, in a parking lot, at a gun show or through an online listing, with no check of any kind. Three decades of survey research puts a number on the gap.

In 1994, 40 percent of gun owners who had recently acquired a firearm did so without a background check, according to the National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, the research Congress had before it when it passed the Brady law. The most recent national estimate, from a 2015 survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, is smaller but still enormous: 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it with no background check. Half of private sales, including sales between individuals, online sales and gun-show sales, closed without one.

The same survey shows what a state law does to that number. In states that regulate private sales, 26 percent of private purchases went unchecked. In states that do not, 57 percent did. Where the law reaches private sales, buyers are screened at more than twice the rate.

The public is not divided on this. In a June 2022 Quinnipiac University national poll, 92 percent of Americans supported requiring background checks for all gun buyers. Few issues in American politics command agreement at that level. The obstacle is not public opinion; it is the Senate calendar.

Universal background checks would not stop every transfer to a person who should not have a gun. They would close the largest documented gap in the system, and they would do it with a mechanism that licensed dealers already run millions of times a year.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, meaning 656 separate incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. That is close to two mass shootings every day for a year.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston share more than a body count. They share a weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings: across the 44 deadliest incidents in the research record running from 1981 to 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, the federal assault weapons ban prohibited the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the years before and after, a difference the researchers reported as a relative rate of 0.30. The ban expired in September 2004. The rifles and the magazines returned to the market, and so did the casualties they are designed to produce.

## Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private, online and gun-show sales, and direct licensed dealers to run those checks through a simple, low-cost process available to private sellers.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition on the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and rewrite the definitions by feature and function so the ban covers the models marketed since 2004 and closes the copycat loopholes.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, and require an annual report to Congress, so the evidence base no longer depends on year-to-year budget decisions.
4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants and technical assistance to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis. Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have one. Most of the country still does not.

The gaps described here are not mysteries and they are not new. Congress has closed both before, measured the result, and then let the policies lapse. The evidence is in the record, the public is ahead of the debate, and the next session of Congress can act on all of it.

---

*Data and sourcing for every figure in this brief are in the accompanying data appendix, "Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data Appendix."*

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, and firearms are now the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the licensed-dealer counter. In a national survey, half of private gun sales closed with no background check, and in states that require checks on private sales the unchecked share is less than half the share in states that do not.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings, from Uvalde and Parkland to Lewiston, and mass-shooting deaths were 70 percent less likely during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 people in the United States were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. That is one death every 11 minutes, around the clock, for a full year.

Behind the count are classrooms with empty desks, youth teams that retired a jersey, and families who now organize their lives around an absence. This is not a statistic that belongs to someone else. It is the background condition of American childhood, and it is not the same everywhere: firearms deaths among children and teens ages 1 to 19 run from 1.2 per 100,000 in Massachusetts to 16.1 per 100,000 in Louisiana.

Nothing about that range is natural. Death rates that differ by a factor of 13 inside one country reflect different rules, different enforcement and different political choices, not different children. The two policies in this brief are among the most consequential of those choices, and both have already been tested in the United States. The country knows what happened when it required background checks on dealer sales and restricted assault weapons, and it knows what happened when it stopped.

## 2. Children and teens

In 2023, 2,566 children ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed, an average of seven every day. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death for this age group, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses. For children and teens ages 1 to 19, the death rate was 5.9 per 100,000 across 2021 to 2023.

Seven children a day is a number most readers will want to reject and cannot. It counts children killed in their own homes and on their own blocks, children who found an unsecured weapon, and teenagers whose crises turned fatal in seconds because a firearm was within reach. Some of those losses have names the whole country knows: the 19 students and two teachers killed at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, the 17 people killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, and the 18 people killed in Lewiston in a single evening in 2023.

These deaths are not evenly distributed, and the states with the lowest rates are not lucky. They are governed. Where a state has put gun safety laws in place, requiring a background check on every sale, giving families a court to turn to when someone is in crisis, and restricting the weapons built to kill many people quickly, fewer children die. The rest of this brief sets out the two federal policies that would move those protections from a patchwork of state laws to the whole country.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady law took effect in 1994, every firearm sale by a licensed dealer has required a background check. The requirement stops at the dealer's counter. In most states a private seller may hand a gun to a stranger, at a kitchen table, in a parking lot, at a gun show or through an online listing, with no check of any kind. Three decades of survey research puts a number on the gap.

In 1994, 40 percent of gun owners who had recently acquired a firearm did so without a background check, according to the National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, the national survey that produced the benchmark estimate of the unchecked share. The most recent national estimate, from a 2015 survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, is smaller but still enormous: 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it with no background check. Half of private sales, including sales between individuals, online sales and gun-show sales, closed without one.

The same survey shows what a state law does to that number. In states that regulate private sales, 26 percent of private purchases went unchecked. In states that do not, 57 percent did. Where the law reaches private sales, buyers are screened at more than twice the rate.

The public is not divided on this. In a June 2022 Quinnipiac University national poll, 92 percent of Americans supported requiring background checks for all gun buyers. Few issues in American politics command agreement at that level. The obstacle is not public opinion; it is the Senate calendar.

Universal background checks would not stop every transfer to a person who should not have a gun. They would close the largest documented gap in the system, and they would do it with a mechanism that licensed dealers already run millions of times a year.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, meaning 656 separate incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. That is close to two mass shootings every day for a year.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston share more than a body count. They share a weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings: across the 44 deadliest incidents in the research record running from 1981 to 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, the federal assault weapons ban prohibited the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the years before and after, a difference the researchers reported as a relative rate of 0.30. The ban expired in September 2004. The rifles and the magazines returned to the market, and so did the casualties they are designed to produce.

## Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private, online and gun-show sales, and direct licensed dealers to run those checks through a simple, low-cost process available to private sellers.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition on the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and rewrite the definitions by feature and function so the ban covers the models marketed since 2004 and closes the copycat loopholes.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, and require an annual report to Congress, so the evidence base no longer depends on year-to-year budget decisions.
4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants and technical assistance to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis. Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have one. Most of the country still does not.

The gaps described here are not mysteries and they are not new. Congress has closed both before, measured the result, and then let the policies lapse. The evidence is in the record, the public is ahead of the debate, and the next session of Congress can act on all of it.

---

*Data and sourcing for every figure in this brief are in the accompanying data appendix, "Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data Appendix."*

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data appendix

**"Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban"**
Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026 | Publication draft

Every figure used in the brief appears below, one table per figure. House figures carry the series source line; where a figure comes from a survey, an incident archive or a poll rather than federal data, the precise citation is given so the appendix can stand on its own.

**Series source line (style sheet rev. 4, B6):** Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.

---

## A1. Total gun deaths, United States, 2023

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| People killed by gun violence, 2023 | 46,728 |
| Frequency | One death every 11 minutes |
| Rank in the historical record | Third-highest annual total on record |

Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research. CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death, 2023; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025.
Note: total firearm deaths of any intent. Per campaign style, the brief does not break the toll out by intent.

## A2. Children and teens

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Children ages 1 to 17 shot and killed, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Average per day, 2023 | 7 |
| Leading cause of death, ages 1 to 17 | Firearms, fourth consecutive year |
| Firearm death rate, children and teens ages 1 to 19, 2021 to 2023 | 5.9 per 100,000 |
| Lowest state, ages 1 to 19 | Massachusetts, 1.2 per 100,000 |
| Highest state, ages 1 to 19 | Louisiana, 16.1 per 100,000 |

Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research. CDC WONDER; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025 (ages 1 to 17); America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Firearm Deaths: Children," CDC WONDER 2021 to 2023 (rate and state range, ages 1 to 19).
Note: "children" means ages 1 to 17; "children and teens" means ages 1 to 19, firearm injuries of any intent. Daily average calculated as 2,566 divided by 365.

## A3. The background-check gap

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Gun owners who acquired a firearm without a background check, 1994 | 40 percent |
| Owners whose most recent firearm, acquired in the prior two years, involved no background check, 2015 survey | 22 percent (95% CI 16 to 27) |
| Private sales obtained without a background check, 2015 survey | 50 percent (95% CI 35 to 65) |
| Private purchases unchecked, states that regulate private sales | 26 percent (95% CI 5 to 47) |
| Private purchases unchecked, states that do not regulate private sales | 57 percent (95% CI 40 to 75) |
| Survey respondents | 1,613 gun owners |

Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, "Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey," Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017 (2015 national survey). The 1994 figure is from Cook and Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, as characterized in the 2017 study.
Note: the 1994 figure covers firearm acquisitions, including gifts and inheritances, not sales alone; the 2015 survey asked directly about background checks.

## A4. Mass shootings, 2023

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass shootings, 2023 | 656 |
| People killed in those incidents | 712 |
| People injured in those incidents | 2,692 |
| Average per day | 1.8 |

Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research; Gun Violence Archive, "Mass Shootings" report, 2023 data (compiled January 2024).
Note: a mass shooting is counted as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter. Daily average calculated as 656 divided by 365.

## A5. Assault weapons and mass-shooting deaths

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| High-fatality mass shootings in the study record, 1981 to 2017 | 44 incidents |
| People killed in those incidents | 501 |
| Deaths caused by assault rifles | 430 (85.8 percent; 95% CI 82.8 to 88.9) |
| Likelihood of a mass-shooting fatality during the federal ban years | 70 percent less likely (relative rate 0.30; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.39) |
| Federal assault weapons ban in force | Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004 |

Source: DiMaggio, Avraham, Lau and Frangos, "Changes in US mass shooting deaths associated with the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban: Analysis of open-source data," Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019.
Note: the 44 incidents are the high-fatality mass shootings analyzed in the study; described as the "deadliest" incidents in the brief and fact sheet. "Assault weapons" is used in the brief for the category covered by the 1994 federal ban, semiautomatic firearms with detachable magazines and defined military-style features, together with large-capacity magazines.

## A6. Public support for background checks

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Support requiring background checks for all gun buyers | 92 percent |
| Oppose | 7 percent |

Source: Quinnipiac University national poll of adults, June 8, 2022.

## A7. Named incidents referenced in the brief

| Incident | Date | People killed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, Texas | May 24, 2022 | 21 (19 students and 2 teachers) |
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Florida | Feb. 14, 2018 | 17 |
| Lewiston, Maine | Oct. 25, 2023 | 18 |

Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research; incident casualty counts from contemporaneous reporting: The Washington Post, Oct. 26, 2023 (Uvalde); Bangor Daily News, Oct. 26, 2023 (Parkland); AP News, Oct. 27, 2023 (Lewiston).

## A8. State extreme-risk protection order laws

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| States with an extreme-risk protection order law in force | 22 states plus the District of Columbia |
| States without one | 28 |

Source: National ERPO Resource Center, "State-by-State," February 2026.
Note: the U.S. Virgin Islands has also enacted an extreme-risk protection order law.

---

**Chart production note:** Charts built from these tables use the series palette, NPI teal #0F6E6E and coral #E4572E. For the rate measures in A2, production recommends a zero-based y-axis so the state-to-state comparison reads at true scale; confirm with the Director of Publications before release.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Fact sheet

**Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026 | For use by Hill offices
Embargoed until Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET

**The ask:** Pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund CDC and NIH gun violence research, and provide grants to states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws.

## Eight statistics for the record

**1. 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023.** One person every 11 minutes; the third-highest annual total on record.
Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research. CDC WONDER, 2023; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025.

**2. Firearms are the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 17, for the fourth consecutive year.** 2,566 children were shot and killed in 2023, an average of seven a day.
Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research. CDC WONDER, 2023; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**3. The firearm death rate for children and teens ages 1 to 19 is 5.9 per 100,000.** The rate ranges from 1.2 per 100,000 in Massachusetts to 16.1 per 100,000 in Louisiana.
Source: America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Firearm Deaths: Children," CDC WONDER, 2021 to 2023.

**4. Half of private gun sales happen without a background check.** In a national survey, 50 percent of private sales, including online and gun-show sales, closed with no check; 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years obtained it with no check.
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, "Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey," Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**5. State laws cut the unchecked share by more than half.** In states that regulate private sales, 26 percent of private purchases went unchecked, against 57 percent in states that do not.
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**6. There were 656 mass shootings in 2023.** 712 people killed and 2,692 injured in incidents where four or more people were shot.
Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research; Gun Violence Archive, "Mass Shootings" report, 2023.

**7. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings.** Assault rifles caused 430 of the 501 deaths, 86 percent, in the 44 deadliest incidents on the 1981 to 2017 record.
Source: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019.

**8. Mass-shooting deaths were 70 percent less likely during the federal assault weapons ban.** Relative rate 0.30 for the 1994 to 2004 ban years against the years before and after.
Source: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019.

## Also on the record

- 92 percent of Americans support requiring background checks for all gun buyers. Source: Quinnipiac University national poll, June 8, 2022.
- 22 states and the District of Columbia have enacted extreme-risk protection order laws. Source: National ERPO Resource Center, February 2026.

**Contact for briefing requests:** Office of the Director of Publications, Northgate Progress Institute.
Full sourcing: see the Brief No. 9 data appendix.
The package is complete and internally consistent. Submitting with full editorial flags:

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, and firearms are now the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the licensed-dealer counter. In a national survey, half of private gun sales closed with no background check, and in states that require checks on private sales the unchecked share is less than half the share in states that do not.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings, from Uvalde and Parkland to Lewiston, and mass-shooting deaths were 70 percent less likely during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 people in the United States were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. That is one death every 11 minutes, around the clock, for a full year.

Behind the count are classrooms with empty desks, youth teams that retired a jersey, and families who now organize their lives around an absence. This is not a statistic that belongs to someone else. It is the background condition of American childhood, and it is not the same everywhere: firearms deaths among children and teens ages 1 to 19 run from 1.2 per 100,000 in Massachusetts to 16.1 per 100,000 in Louisiana.

Nothing about that range is natural. Death rates that differ by a factor of 13 inside one country reflect different rules, different enforcement and different political choices, not different children. The two policies in this brief are among the most consequential of those choices, and both have already been tested in the United States. The country knows what happened when it required background checks on dealer sales and restricted assault weapons, and it knows what happened when it stopped.

## 2. Children and teens

In 2023, 2,566 children ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed, an average of seven every day. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death for this age group, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses. For children and teens ages 1 to 19, the death rate was 5.9 per 100,000 across 2021 to 2023.

Seven children a day is a number most readers will want to reject and cannot. It counts children killed in their own homes and on their own blocks, children who found an unsecured weapon, and teenagers whose crises turned fatal in seconds because a firearm was within reach. Some of those losses have names the whole country knows: the 19 students and two teachers killed at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, the 17 people killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, and the 18 people killed in Lewiston in a single evening in 2023.

These deaths are not evenly distributed, and the states with the lowest rates are not lucky. They are governed. Where a state has put gun safety laws in place, requiring a background check on every sale, giving families a court to turn to when someone is in crisis, and restricting the weapons built to kill many people quickly, fewer children die. The rest of this brief sets out the two federal policies that would move those protections from a patchwork of state laws to the whole country.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady law took effect in 1994, every firearm sale by a licensed dealer has required a background check. The requirement stops at the dealer's counter. In most states a private seller may hand a gun to a stranger, at a kitchen table, in a parking lot, at a gun show or through an online listing, with no check of any kind. Three decades of survey research puts a number on the gap.

In 1994, 40 percent of gun owners who had recently acquired a firearm did so without a background check, according to the National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, the national survey that produced the benchmark estimate of the unchecked share. The most recent national estimate, from a 2015 survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, is smaller but still enormous: 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it with no background check. Half of private sales, including sales between individuals, online sales and gun-show sales, closed without one.

The same survey shows what a state law does to that number. In states that regulate private sales, 26 percent of private purchases went unchecked. In states that do not, 57 percent did. Where the law reaches private sales, unchecked sales are less than half as common.

The public is not divided on this. In a June 2022 Quinnipiac University national poll, 92 percent of Americans supported requiring background checks for all gun buyers. Few issues in American politics command agreement at that level. The obstacle is not public opinion; it is the Senate calendar.

Universal background checks would not stop every transfer to a person who should not have a gun. They would close the largest documented gap in the system, and they would do it with a mechanism that licensed dealers already run millions of times a year.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, meaning 656 separate incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. That is close to two mass shootings every day for a year.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston share more than a body count. They share a class of weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings: across the 44 deadliest incidents in the research record running from 1981 to 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, the federal assault weapons ban prohibited the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the years before and after, a difference the researchers reported as a relative rate of 0.30. The ban expired in September 2004. The rifles and the magazines returned to the market, and so did the casualties they are designed to produce.

## Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private, online and gun-show sales, and direct licensed dealers to run those checks through a simple, low-cost process available to private sellers.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition on the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and rewrite the definitions by feature and function so the ban covers the models marketed since 2004 and closes the copycat loopholes.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, and require an annual report to Congress, so the evidence base no longer depends on year-to-year budget decisions.
4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants and technical assistance to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis. Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have one. Most of the country still does not.

The gaps described here are not mysteries and they are not new. Congress has closed both before, measured the result, and then let the policies lapse. The evidence is in the record, the public is ahead of the debate, and the next session of Congress can act on all of it.

---

*Data and sourcing for every figure in this brief are in the accompanying data appendix, "Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data Appendix."*
